title: Permission-denial tests need effective credentials, not only file mode bits
applies_when: A native filesystem test expects EACCES or os.ErrPermission after chmod, especially on a remote development host or container running as root.
lesson: Check the actual test process's effective UID, groups and relevant capabilities before diagnosing a permission failure as a product regression. CAP_DAC_OVERRIDE and CAP_DAC_READ_SEARCH can bypass checks that the test expects to fail. A root run can therefore make the operation succeed; an assertion that calls Error() on the resulting nil error may then panic, hiding the environmental cause. Preserve that failure and rerun unchanged source with appropriate nonprivileged credentials, a writable task-private source/cache/temp tree and the same dependency/toolchain identities. Verify tracked source and locks afterward. Do not skip the permission test, weaken its expected error, or chmod shared/private environments just to make a baseline green.
avoid_when: A nonzero UID alone does not prove that bypass capabilities are absent, and UID 0 alone does not prove which capabilities a container retains. Do not reclassify an unrelated race or functional failure merely because root is involved. A nonprivileged identity is not a sandbox for untrusted repository code; keep the separate execution authority and isolation assessment.

evidence.note: Linux documents CAP_DAC_OVERRIDE and CAP_DAC_READ_SEARCH as bypasses for discretionary file permission checks; effective credentials are an input to test semantics. This is mechanism evidence, not measured Scout utility.

TestFailGenFishCompletionFile creates a mode-0400 file, expects os.ErrPermission and calls got.Error() in the unexpected-result branch. Read this exact caller before attributing its panic to completion generation; this source does not establish a production vulnerability or the entire Go/OS test matrix.
